content.text: This is a full R package with a vignette. Let me read the README and vignette to understand the intended workflow for inferring cell-cell communication from bulk expression data.

content.content: 1 RaCInG 2 ================ 3 4 [![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml) 5 [![pkgdown](https://github.com/VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package/actions/workflows/pkgdown.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package/actions/workflows/pkgdown.yaml) 6 7 **RaCInG** (**Ra**ndom **C**ell-cell **In**teraction **G**enerator) 8 reconstructs patient-specific cell-cell communication networks from bulk 9 RNA-seq data and extracts network-level features using either a 10 kernel-based or Monte Carlo workflow. 11 12 This package is the R implementation of the [original RaCInG Python 13 framework](https://github.com/SysBioOncology/RaCInG), as described in 14 [van Santvoort et 15 al. (2025)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39954673/), repackaged for 16 seamless integration with R/Bioconductor analysis pipelines. It is 17 additionally coupled with 18 [multideconv](https://github.com/VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv) for 19 deconvolution and cell-type subgroup identification, and with 20 [OmnipathR](https://omnipathdb.org/)/[liana](https://saezlab.github.io/liana/) 21 for ligand-receptor prior knowledge. 22 23 ## Installation 24 25 ### Install from GitHub 26 27 ``` r 28 # install.packages("remotes") 29 remotes::install_github("VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package") 30 library(RaCInG) 31 ``` 32 33 ### Install from a local clone 34 35 ``` r 36 # install.packages("devtools") 37 devtools::install(".") 38 ``` 39 40 ### Optional preprocessing dependencies 41 42 If you want to start directly from raw counts with 43 `prepare_input_files()`, install the optional helper packages used 44 during deconvolution and prior-network construction: 45 46 ``` r 47 install.packages(c("ggplot2", "nnls")) 48 # ADImpute and OmnipathR are available from Bioconductor: 49 BiocManager::install(c("ADImpute", "OmnipathR")) 50 # liana and multideconv are GitHub-only: 51 remotes::install_github(c("saezlab/liana", "VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv")) 52 ``` 53 54 ## Workflow at a glance 55 56 | Goal | Function | Output | 57 |--------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------| 58 | Build input matrices from raw counts | `prepare_input_files()` | Named list with `L`, `R`, `C`, `LR` matrices and labels | 59 | Compute direct communication (deterministic) | `compute_racing_kernel()` | Kernel arrays + feature matrix | 60 | Compute direct communication and/or GSCC by simulation | `compute_racing_montecarlo()` | Per-patient mean and sd across simulated graphs | 61 | Decompose a direct score into ligand-receptor pairs | `computeLRContributions()` + `plotLRContributions()` | Ranked contributions and a dot plot | 62 | Compare patient groups | `wilcox_group_test()` + `top_features_plot()` | Statistics table and ranked bar plot | 63 | Relate features to a continuous score | `correlate_features_with_score()` + `correlation_plot()` | Correlation table and rainfall plot | 64 65 ## Quick start 66 67 Try the workflow on the bundled, pre-processed melanoma example (no 68 optional dependencies needed): 69 70 ``` r 71 library(RaCInG) 72 data(skcm_example) 73 74 kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(input_data = skcm_example) 75 head(kernel_res$features) 76 77 # Which ligand-receptor pairs drive Tumor <-> CD8+ T communication? 78 lr <- computeLRContributions( 79 Lmatrix = skcm_example$Lmatrix, Rmatrix = skcm_example$Rmatrix, 80 Cmatrix = skcm_example$Cmatrix, LRmatrix = skcm_example$LRmatrix, 81 celltypes = skcm_example$celltypes, sender = "Tumor", receiver = "CD8+ T" 82 ) 83 plotLRContributions(lr, top_n = 10) 84 ``` 85 86 Or start from your own raw counts: 87 88 ``` r 89 # Build input matrices from a real bulk RNA-seq counts matrix 90 # (bundled with the optional `multideconv` dependency) 91 data(raw_counts, package = "multideconv") 92 counts_matrix <- as.matrix(raw_counts) 93 94 input <- prepare_input_files( 95 counts = counts_matrix, 96 output_folder = "Results/", 97 file_name = "example" 98 ) 99 100 # Run kernel method (from raw counts) 101 kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel( 102 counts = counts_matrix, 103 file_name = "example", 104 output_folder = tempdir(), 105 communication_type = "D" 106 ) 107 108 # Or pass pre-computed inputs to skip preprocessing 109 kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel( 110 input_data = input, 111 communication_type = "D" 112 ) 113 114 # Monte Carlo method 115 mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo( 116 input_data = input, 117 file_name = "example", 118 output_folder = tempdir(), 119 communication_type = c("D", "GSCC"), 120 Ncells = 100, 121 Ngraphs = 10, 122 Ndegree = 3 123 ) 124 125 # Compare clinical groups: one label per patient (replace with your own annotation) 126 grouping <- rep(c("Responder", "Non-responder"), length.out = nrow(kernel_res$features)) 127 wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping) 128 top_features_plot(wilcox_results) 129 ``` 130 131 The kernel method computes direct communication (`"D"`). The Monte Carlo 132 method computes direct communication and/or the giant strongly connected 133 component (`"GSCC"`); requesting both (`c("D", "GSCC")`) extracts them 134 from the same simulated graphs in one call. 135 `compute_racing_montecarlo()` additionally takes `ncores` to parallelize 136 independent patients across cores. 137 138 ## Documentation 139 140 - 📘 Vignette: [Getting started with 141 RaCInG](https://VeraPancaldiLab.github.io/RaCInG_package/articles/RaCiNG.html) 142 - 🌐 Website: 143 - 🐍 Original Python implementation: 144 145 146 ## Citation 147 148 If you use this package, please cite the RaCInG publication: 149 150 > van Santvoort M, Lapuente-Santana Ó, Zopoglou M, Zackl C, Finotello F, 151 > van der Hoorn P & Eduati F (2025). *Mathematically mapping the network 152 > of cells in the tumor microenvironment.* Cell Reports Methods, 5(2), 153 > 100985. 154 155 ## R Package Development 156 157 This R package implementation was developed by [Marcelo 158 Hurtado](https://github.com/mhurtado13) from the [Pancaldi 159 team](https://github.com/VeraPancaldiLab), led by Vera Pancaldi. Marcelo 160 is currently the primary maintainer of the package. 161

1	---
2	title: "Getting started with RaCInG"
3	output:
4	  rmarkdown::html_vignette:
5	    toc: true
6	    number_sections: false
7	vignette: >
8	  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Getting started with RaCInG}
9	  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
10	  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
11	---
12	
13	```{r, include = FALSE}
14	knitr::opts_chunk$set(
15	  collapse = TRUE,
16	  comment = "#>",
17	  fig.width = 7,
18	  fig.height = 4
19	)
20	```
21	
22	## Overview
23	
24	`RaCInG` reconstructs patient-specific cell-cell communication networks from bulk
25	RNA-seq data. The package supports two complementary workflows:
26	
27	- a **kernel-based** approach for fast, deterministic direct-communication
28	  features (`"D"`), and
29	- a **Monte Carlo** approach that simulates networks and reports direct
30	  communication (`"D"`) and/or the giant strongly connected component (`"GSCC"`).
31	
32	This vignette shows the recommended workflow and the most important entry points for
33	new users, using both the bundled, ready-made example data and a real bulk RNA-seq
34	counts matrix run through the full preprocessing pipeline.
35	
36	## Installation
37	
38	### Install from GitHub
39	
40	```{r eval = FALSE}
41	# install.packages("remotes")
42	remotes::install_github("VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package")
43	library(RaCInG)
44	```
45	
46	### Install from a local checkout
47	
48	```{r eval = FALSE}
49	# install.packages("devtools")
50	devtools::install(".")
51	library(RaCInG)
52	```
53	
54	If you want to build the RaCInG input matrices directly from raw counts, install the
55	optional preprocessing dependencies used by `prepare_input_files()`:
56	
57	```{r eval = FALSE}
58	install.packages(c("ggplot2", "nnls"))
59	# ADImpute and OmnipathR are available from Bioconductor:
60	BiocManager::install(c("ADImpute", "OmnipathR"))
61	# liana and multideconv are GitHub-only:
62	remotes::install_github(c("saezlab/liana", "VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv"))
63	```
64	
65	## Workflow at a glance
66	
67	| Goal | Function | Output |
68	| --- | --- | --- |
69	| Build input matrices from raw counts | `prepare_input_files()` | Named list with `L`, `R`, `C`, `LR` matrices and labels |
70	| Compute direct communication (deterministic) | `compute_racing_kernel()` | Kernel arrays + feature matrix |
71	| Compute direct communication and/or GSCC by simulation | `compute_racing_montecarlo()` | Processed Monte Carlo results |
72	| Decompose a direct score into ligand-receptor pairs | `computeLRContributions()` + `plotLRContributions()` | Ranked contributions and a LIANA-style dot plot |
73	| Compare clinical groups | `wilcox_group_test()` + `top_features_plot()` | Statistics table and ranked bar plot |
74	| Relate features to a continuous score | `correlate_features_with_score()` + `correlation_plot()` | Correlation table and rainfall plot |
75	
76	## How `prepare_input_files()` builds its inputs
77	
78	Starting from a raw gene-by-sample counts matrix, `prepare_input_files()` chains
79	together several packages so you never have to run them by hand:
80	
81	1. **Normalization**: counts are converted to TPM with `ADImpute::NormalizeTPM()`.
82	2. **Deconvolution**: cell-type fractions are estimated with
83	   `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` (by default the multideconv set of methods --
84	   Quantiseq, CIBERSORTx, EpiDISH, DeconRNASeq and DWLS -- or any method(s) passed via
85	   `deconv_method`; the examples below use Quantiseq only, to run quickly), which
86	   also standardizes cell-type names to multideconv's vocabulary
87	   (`multideconv::get_cell_type_nomenclature()`).
88	3. **Subgroup analysis**: `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()` (multideconv
89	   >= 0.2.0) clusters highly correlated deconvolution features of the same cell type
90	   (e.g. several methods agreeing on it) into subgroups such as `"B.cells_Subgroup.1"`,
91	   discarding mostly-zero and low-variance features along the way. Features that join
92	   no subgroup keep their full name (e.g. `"Quantiseq_TIL10_B.cells"`); these names
93	   are used as the RaCInG cell types.
94	4. **Cell-type expression profiles**: for every gene, a non-negative least squares
95	   fit of bulk expression against the cell-type fractions of each method-signature
96	   combination gives one expression value per gene per cell type; each subgroup's
97	   profile is the median of its members' profiles.
98	5. **Ligand-receptor prior knowledge**: a curated, OmniPath-backed consensus network
99	   is retrieved with `liana::get_curated_omni()` and restricted to ligand/receptor
100	   roles, then decomplexified into single-gene subunits.
101	6. **Filtering and assembly**: ligand-receptor pairs are kept only where both genes
102	   reach `expr_threshold` (default 10 TPM) in the sending and receiving cell types,
103	   and the `Lmatrix`, `Rmatrix`, `Cmatrix`, and `LRmatrix` inputs (see below) are
104	   assembled and written to `output_folder`. Each ligand-receptor pair's per-patient
105	   strength combines the two genes' bulk `log2(TPM + 1)` expression with `fun_LR`
106	   (default `min`, i.e. the weaker partner limits the interaction).
107	
108	You can skip any of steps 2-5 by supplying your own `deconv`, `cell_expr_profile`,
109	or `cc_network` directly. A user-supplied `deconv` must have exactly
110	`colnames(counts)` as row names, in the same order, and should use multideconv's
111	cell-type nomenclature (a warning lists any names outside it). If your expression
112	data is already linear-scale TPM rather than raw counts, pass
113	`already_normalized = TRUE`; log-scale data (e.g. `log2(TPM + 1)`) must be converted
114	back first (`2^x - 1`), since `expr_threshold` is compared on the linear scale.
115	
116	## Recommended workflow with a real bulk RNA-seq dataset
117	
118	The examples below use the raw bulk RNA-seq counts matrix bundled with the
119	`multideconv` package (`raw_counts`, from Mariathasan et al. 2018, a
120	urothelial/bladder cancer cohort profiled for anti-PD-L1 response) to exercise the
121	full pipeline end to end, from raw counts to features to statistics. These chunks
122	call out to the network (OmniPath/LIANA) and run real deconvolution, so they are
123	shown but not evaluated when the vignette is built; run them interactively to try
124	the full pipeline yourself.
125	
126	### 1. Build input matrices from raw counts
127	
128	```{r eval = FALSE}
129	data(raw_counts, package = "multideconv")
130	counts_matrix <- as.matrix(raw_counts)
131	
132	input <- prepare_input_files(
133	  counts = counts_matrix,
134	  output_folder = "Results/",
135	  file_name = "mariathasan",
136	  deconv_method = "Quantiseq"
137	)
138	
139	str(input, max.level = 1)
140	input$celltypes
141	```
142	
143	### 2. Run the kernel method
144	
145	The kernel method is the fastest way to derive direct communication features
146	(`communication_type = "D"`, the only type it computes) across patients.
147	You can pass `counts` to let the function compute inputs
148	automatically, or supply previously computed matrices via `input_data`.
149	
150	```{r eval = FALSE}
151	# Option A: from raw counts (runs prepare_input_files internally)
152	kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
153	  counts = counts_matrix,
154	  output_folder = tempdir(),
155	  file_name = "mariathasan",
156	  communication_type = "D",
157	  norm = TRUE
158	)
159	
160	# Option B: from pre-computed input matrices (skips preprocessing)
161	kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
162	  input_data = input,
163	  communication_type = "D",
164	  norm = TRUE
165	)
166	
167	head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])
168	```
169	
170	Features are named `"Dir_A_B"`, with the lower-index (alphabetically first) cell
171	type first; with `remove_direction = TRUE` (the default) the two directions of each
172	pair are summed into one feature. Feature columns with no possible ligand-receptor
173	pathway in any patient (structurally zero for every patient) are dropped
174	automatically, rather than returned as dead all-zero columns -- so
175	`ncol(kernel_res$features)` is usually well below the full combinatorial count of
176	cell-type pairs. Lower `zero_threshold` (e.g. `0.9`) to also drop features that are
177	zero in most patients.
178	
179	#### Raw or normalized features?
180	
181	With `norm = FALSE` (the default) features are the raw communication strength, which
182	grows with both the abundance of the two cell types and the expression of their
183	ligand-receptor pairs. With `norm = TRUE`, RaCInG also builds a baseline in which
184	every possible ligand-receptor pair is equally strong and reports the ratio of the
185	two: an enrichment score that does not depend on cell-type abundance and isolates
186	which pairs communicate more (or less) than the network structure alone predicts.
187	In the Monte Carlo method the ratio of two simulated estimates is noisier than the
188	raw value, so budget a larger `Ngraphs` when you use `norm = TRUE` there.
189	
190	### 3. Run the Monte Carlo method
191	
192	Use the Monte Carlo workflow when you want simulation-based summaries or uncertainty
193	estimates from repeated graph realizations. The same `input_data` shortcut is
194	available here. Simulation cost scales with `Ncells` and `Ngraphs`; the values below
195	are kept small for a quick illustration.
196	
197	```{r eval = FALSE}
198	set.seed(1)
199	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
200	  counts = counts_matrix,
201	  output_folder = tempdir(),
202	  deconv_method = "Quantiseq",
203	  file_name = "mariathasan",
204	  nPatients = 3,
205	  communication_type = "D",
206	  Ncells = 100,
207	  Ngraphs = 10,
208	  Ndegree = 3,
209	  norm = TRUE
210	)
211	
212	# Or from pre-computed inputs:
213	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
214	  input_data = input,
215	  output_folder = tempdir(),
216	  file_name = "mariathasan",
217	  communication_type = "D",
218	  Ncells = 100,
219	  Ngraphs = 10,
220	  Ndegree = 3,
221	  norm = TRUE
222	)
223	
224	head(mc_res$output$mean[, 1:5])
225	```
226	
227	`mc_res$output` holds the per-patient mean (`mean`) and standard deviation (`sd`)
228	across the simulated graphs. The raw simulations (`<file_name>.out`, and
229	`<file_name>_norm.out` with `norm = TRUE`) and the processed features
230	(`<file_name>.csv`, `<file_name>_sd.csv`) are also written to `output_folder`; they
231	can be re-read later with `Read_Sim_Output()` and `compute_results_processing()`.
232	
233	`communication_type` can also be `"GSCC"` (the share of cells, per cell type, in the
234	giant strongly connected component) or both, `c("D", "GSCC")`. Both are then
235	extracted from the *same* simulated graphs, instead of re-simulating a fresh set of
236	graphs per type -- graph generation, not feature extraction, is the expensive part of
237	a Monte Carlo run:
238	
239	```{r eval = FALSE}
240	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
241	  input_data = input,
242	  communication_type = c("D", "GSCC"),
243	  Ncells = 100,
244	  Ngraphs = 10,
245	  Ndegree = 3,
246	  norm = TRUE,
247	  output_folder = tempdir(),
248	  file_name = "mariathasan"
249	)
250	
251	# output is now a named list, one entry per requested type
252	names(mc_res$output)
253	head(mc_res$output$D$mean[, 1:5])
254	```
255	
256	Patients are independent of each other, so larger runs can be parallelized across
257	cores with `ncores` (via `parallel`/`doParallel`/`foreach`, so it works the same way
258	on Windows, macOS, and Linux):
259	
260	```{r eval = FALSE}
261	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
262	  input_data = input,
263	  communication_type = "D",
264	  Ncells = 500,
265	  Ngraphs = 100,
266	  Ndegree = 20,
267	  ncores = 4,
268	  output_folder = tempdir(),
269	  file_name = "mariathasan"
270	)
271	```
272	
273	### 4. Compare clinical groups
274	
275	Once features are available in a patient-by-feature matrix, use the built-in Wilcoxon
276	workflow to compare groups. `wilcox_group_test()` reports, per feature and per pair
277	of groups, the Wilcoxon statistic, fold change, and (jointly) FDR-adjusted p-value;
278	`top_features_plot()` shows the top up/down features by `log2(fold change)` as a
279	ranked bar chart.
280	
281	```{r eval = FALSE}
282	# One label per patient (row of the feature matrix); replace this placeholder
283	# with your own clinical annotation, e.g. response to therapy.
284	grouping <- rep(c("Responder", "Non-responder"), length.out = nrow(kernel_res$features))
285	wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
286	head(wilcox_results)
287	top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 15)
288	```
289	
290	With more than two groups, every pairwise comparison is run automatically; subset
291	`wilcox_results` by `Comparison` (or pass a two-group subset to `top_features_plot()`) to
292	inspect one pair at a time.
293	
294	### 5. Correlate features with a continuous score
295	
296	If you have a continuous per-patient score (e.g. an immune response or survival
297	score), `correlate_features_with_score()` reports the Spearman correlation between
298	every feature and the score, pooled across all patients and, optionally, within
299	groups. `correlation_plot()` shows the top positive and negative correlations.
300	
301	```{r eval = FALSE}
302	response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
303	corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
304	head(corr_results)
305	correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)
306	```
307	
308	## Understanding the input files
309	
310	RaCInG requires four matrices and associated label vectors that describe the
311	cell-cell communication landscape for a cohort of patients. The table below
312	summarises each component:
313	
314	| Component | Dimensions | Description |
315	| --- | --- | --- |
316	| **Lmatrix** | cell types × ligands | Binary compatibility matrix: `1` if that ligand is expressed above `expr_threshold` in that cell type, `0` otherwise. Rows are cell types; columns are ligands. |
317	| **Rmatrix** | cell types × receptors | Binary compatibility matrix: `1` if that receptor is expressed above `expr_threshold` in that cell type, `0` otherwise. Same row order as `Lmatrix`. |
318	| **Cmatrix** | patients × cell types | Cell-type fraction for each patient. Each row sums to 1. |
319	| **LRmatrix** | ligands × receptors × patients | 3-D tensor of ligand–receptor interaction weights. Each patient slice is normalised to sum to 1. |
320	| **celltypes** | character vector | Alphabetically sorted cell-type names (shared across L, R, and C). |
321	| **ligands** | character vector | Ligand names matching the columns of `Lmatrix` and the first axis of `LRmatrix`. |
322	| **receptors** | character vector | Receptor names matching the columns of `Rmatrix` and the second axis of `LRmatrix`. |
323	| **Sign_matrix** | ligands × receptors | Placeholder for stimulatory (+1) / inhibitory (−1) interaction signs; all zeros (unknown) by default. Not used by the current kernel or Monte Carlo features. |
324	
325	These inputs are typically generated by `prepare_input_files()` from a raw
326	counts matrix, or they can be assembled manually from pre-existing deconvolution
327	and prior-network data. The bundled `skcm_example` dataset provides a ready-made
328	example of this structure.
329	
330	### Inspecting the example inputs
331	
332	```{r}
333	library(RaCInG)
334	data(skcm_example)
335	
336	# Overall structure
337	str(skcm_example, max.level = 1)
338	```
339	
340	```{r}
341	# Lmatrix: 9 cell types × 276 ligands
342	dim(skcm_example$Lmatrix)
343	skcm_example$Lmatrix[1:4, 1:5]
344	```
345	
346	```{r}
347	# Rmatrix: 9 cell types × 298 receptors
348	dim(skcm_example$Rmatrix)
349	skcm_example$Rmatrix[1:4, 1:5]
350	```
351	
352	```{r}
353	# Cmatrix: 10 patients × 9 cell types (rows sum to 1)
354	dim(skcm_example$Cmatrix)
355	skcm_example$Cmatrix[1:4, ]
356	```
357	
358	```{r}
359	# LRmatrix: 276 ligands × 298 receptors × 10 patients (3-D tensor)
360	dim(skcm_example$LRmatrix)
361	# First patient slice, top-left corner:
362	skcm_example$LRmatrix[1:4, 1:4, 1]
363	```
364	
365	```{r}
366	# Label vectors
367	skcm_example$celltypes
368	head(skcm_example$ligands, 10)
369	head(skcm_example$receptors, 10)
370	```
371	
372	## Running with the bundled example data
373	
374	The `skcm_example` list shown above can be passed directly to the kernel or Monte
375	Carlo workflows via the `input_data` parameter, and to the statistical analysis
376	functions once features have been computed.
377	
378	### Kernel method on the example data
379	
380	```{r}
381	kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
382	  input_data   = skcm_example,
383	  output_folder = tempdir(),
384	  communication_type = "D",
385	  norm = TRUE
386	)
387	
388	head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])
389	```
390	
391	### Decomposing a score into ligand-receptor pairs
392	
393	`compute_kernel()` sums over every ligand-receptor pair to produce one score per
394	cell-type pair, so that score alone can't tell you which ligand-receptor pairs drove
395	it. `computeLRContributions()` recovers that breakdown for one sender-receiver pair
396	(exploiting that the kernel formula is linear in `LRmatrix`, so each pair's
397	contribution can be computed directly and sums back exactly to the original score),
398	and `plotLRContributions()` shows the top contributors as a LIANA-style dot plot (dot
399	size = share of that pair's total score, color = raw contribution).
400	
401	```{r, fig.alt = "Dot plot of the top ligand-receptor pairs contributing to Tumor and CD8+ T communication, per patient; dot size is the share of the total score and color the raw contribution."}
402	lr_contrib <- computeLRContributions(
403	  Lmatrix = skcm_example$Lmatrix, Rmatrix = skcm_example$Rmatrix,
404	  Cmatrix = skcm_example$Cmatrix, LRmatrix = skcm_example$LRmatrix,
405	  celltypes = skcm_example$celltypes, sender = "Tumor", receiver = "CD8+ T"
406	)
407	head(lr_contrib)
408	plotLRContributions(lr_contrib, top_n = 10)
409	```
410	
411	### Statistical analysis on the example data
412	
413	The example data has no clinical annotation, so for illustration patients are split
414	by their CD8+ T-cell infiltration (above vs below the median). In your own data, use
415	a real clinical variable such as response to therapy. (With only 10 patients many
416	values are tied, so `wilcox.test()` warns that it cannot compute exact p-values;
417	those warnings are hidden here.)
418	
419	```{r, warning = FALSE, fig.alt = "Ranked bar chart of the direct-communication features most up- and down-regulated in CD8-high versus CD8-low patients."}
420	cd8 <- skcm_example$Cmatrix[, "CD8+ T"]
421	grouping <- ifelse(cd8 > median(cd8), "CD8_high", "CD8_low")
422	wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
423	head(wilcox_results)
424	top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 10)
425	```
426	
427	For a continuous score, a random placeholder is used below; replace it with a
428	per-patient score of your own (e.g. an immune-response signature).
429	
430	```{r, fig.alt = "Diverging bar chart of the features with the strongest positive and negative Spearman correlations with the score."}
431	set.seed(1)
432	response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
433	corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
434	head(corr_results)
435	correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)
436	```
437	
438	### Monte Carlo method on the example data
439	
440	The settings below are deliberately tiny so the example runs in seconds; real
441	analyses use thousands of cells (`Ncells`) and around 100 graphs (`Ngraphs`) per
442	patient.
443	
444	```{r}
445	set.seed(42)
446	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
447	  input_data   = skcm_example,
448	  output_folder = tempdir(),
449	  file_name     = "skcm_example",
450	  nPatients     = 2,
451	  communication_type = c("D", "GSCC"),
452	  Ncells  = 100,
453	  Ngraphs = 5,
454	  Ndegree = 3
455	)
456	
457	# Direct communication: mean and standard deviation across the simulated graphs
458	head(mc_res$output$D$mean[, 1:5])
459	head(mc_res$output$D$sd[, 1:5])
460	
461	# Fraction of all cells that belong to the GSCC, per cell type
462	mc_res$output$GSCC$mean
463	```
464	
465	## Notes
466	
467	- `compute_racing_kernel()` and `compute_racing_montecarlo()` are the main entry points.
468	- The kernel method computes direct communication only; GSCC is available with the
469	  Monte Carlo method. Wedges and triangles are no longer part of RaCInG.
470	- Both accept an `input_data` argument with pre-computed matrices (as returned by
471	  `prepare_input_files()`), which skips all preprocessing.
472	- `prepare_input_files()` requires the optional packages listed under Installation
473	  for deconvolution and prior-network assembly.
474	- The original Python implementation is available at
475	  <https://github.com/SysBioOncology/RaCInG>.
476

---
title: "Getting started with RaCInG"
output:
  rmarkdown::html_vignette:
    toc: true
    number_sections: false
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Getting started with RaCInG}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
```

## Overview

`RaCInG` reconstructs patient-specific cell-cell communication networks from bulk
RNA-seq data. The package supports two complementary workflows:

- a **kernel-based** approach for fast, deterministic direct-communication
  features (`"D"`), and
- a **Monte Carlo** approach that simulates networks and reports direct
  communication (`"D"`) and/or the giant strongly connected component (`"GSCC"`).

This vignette shows the recommended workflow and the most important entry points for
new users, using both the bundled, ready-made example data and a real bulk RNA-seq
counts matrix run through the full preprocessing pipeline.

## Installation

### Install from GitHub

```{r eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package")
library(RaCInG)
```

### Install from a local checkout

```{r eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install(".")
library(RaCInG)
```

If you want to build the RaCInG input matrices directly from raw counts, install the
optional preprocessing dependencies used by `prepare_input_files()`:

```{r eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "nnls"))
# ADImpute and OmnipathR are available from Bioconductor:
BiocManager::install(c("ADImpute", "OmnipathR"))
# liana and multideconv are GitHub-only:
remotes::install_github(c("saezlab/liana", "VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv"))
```

## Workflow at a glance

| Goal | Function | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build input matrices from raw counts | `prepare_input_files()` | Named list with `L`, `R`, `C`, `LR` matrices and labels |
| Compute direct communication (deterministic) | `compute_racing_kernel()` | Kernel arrays + feature matrix |
| Compute direct communication and/or GSCC by simulation | `compute_racing_montecarlo()` | Processed Monte Carlo results |
| Decompose a direct score into ligand-receptor pairs | `computeLRContributions()` + `plotLRContributions()` | Ranked contributions and a LIANA-style dot plot |
| Compare clinical groups | `wilcox_group_test()` + `top_features_plot()` | Statistics table and ranked bar plot |
| Relate features to a continuous score | `correlate_features_with_score()` + `correlation_plot()` | Correlation table and rainfall plot |

## How `prepare_input_files()` builds its inputs

Starting from a raw gene-by-sample counts matrix, `prepare_input_files()` chains
together several packages so you never have to run them by hand:

1. **Normalization**: counts are converted to TPM with `ADImpute::NormalizeTPM()`.
2. **Deconvolution**: cell-type fractions are estimated with
   `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` (by default the multideconv set of methods --
   Quantiseq, CIBERSORTx, EpiDISH, DeconRNASeq and DWLS -- or any method(s) passed via
   `deconv_method`; the examples below use Quantiseq only, to run quickly), which
   also standardizes cell-type names to multideconv's vocabulary
   (`multideconv::get_cell_type_nomenclature()`).
3. **Subgroup analysis**: `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()` (multideconv
   >= 0.2.0) clusters highly correlated deconvolution features of the same cell type
   (e.g. several methods agreeing on it) into subgroups such as `"B.cells_Subgroup.1"`,
   discarding mostly-zero and low-variance features along the way. Features that join
   no subgroup keep their full name (e.g. `"Quantiseq_TIL10_B.cells"`); these names
   are used as the RaCInG cell types.
4. **Cell-type expression profiles**: for every gene, a non-negative least squares
   fit of bulk expression against the cell-type fractions of each method-signature
   combination gives one expression value per gene per cell type; each subgroup's
   profile is the median of its members' profiles.
5. **Ligand-receptor prior knowledge**: a curated, OmniPath-backed consensus network
   is retrieved with `liana::get_curated_omni()` and restricted to ligand/receptor
   roles, then decomplexified into single-gene subunits.
6. **Filtering and assembly**: ligand-receptor pairs are kept only where both genes
   reach `expr_threshold` (default 10 TPM) in the sending and receiving cell types,
   and the `Lmatrix`, `Rmatrix`, `Cmatrix`, and `LRmatrix` inputs (see below) are
   assembled and written to `output_folder`. Each ligand-receptor pair's per-patient
   strength combines the two genes' bulk `log2(TPM + 1)` expression with `fun_LR`
   (default `min`, i.e. the weaker partner limits the interaction).

You can skip any of steps 2-5 by supplying your own `deconv`, `cell_expr_profile`,
or `cc_network` directly. A user-supplied `deconv` must have exactly
`colnames(counts)` as row names, in the same order, and should use multideconv's
cell-type nomenclature (a warning lists any names outside it). If your expression
data is already linear-scale TPM rather than raw counts, pass
`already_normalized = TRUE`; log-scale data (e.g. `log2(TPM + 1)`) must be converted
back first (`2^x - 1`), since `expr_threshold` is compared on the linear scale.

## Recommended workflow with a real bulk RNA-seq dataset

The examples below use the raw bulk RNA-seq counts matrix bundled with the
`multideconv` package (`raw_counts`, from Mariathasan et al. 2018, a
urothelial/bladder cancer cohort profiled for anti-PD-L1 response) to exercise the
full pipeline end to end, from raw counts to features to statistics. These chunks
call out to the network (OmniPath/LIANA) and run real deconvolution, so they are
shown but not evaluated when the vignette is built; run them interactively to try
the full pipeline yourself.

### 1. Build input matrices from raw counts

```{r eval = FALSE}
data(raw_counts, package = "multideconv")
counts_matrix <- as.matrix(raw_counts)

input <- prepare_input_files(
  counts = counts_matrix,
  output_folder = "Results/",
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  deconv_method = "Quantiseq"
)

str(input, max.level = 1)
input$celltypes
```

### 2. Run the kernel method

The kernel method is the fastest way to derive direct communication features
(`communication_type = "D"`, the only type it computes) across patients.
You can pass `counts` to let the function compute inputs
automatically, or supply previously computed matrices via `input_data`.

```{r eval = FALSE}
# Option A: from raw counts (runs prepare_input_files internally)
kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  counts = counts_matrix,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  communication_type = "D",
  norm = TRUE
)

# Option B: from pre-computed input matrices (skips preprocessing)
kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = "D",
  norm = TRUE
)

head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])
```

Features are named `"Dir_A_B"`, with the lower-index (alphabetically first) cell
type first; with `remove_direction = TRUE` (the default) the two directions of each
pair are summed into one feature. Feature columns with no possible ligand-receptor
pathway in any patient (structurally zero for every patient) are dropped
automatically, rather than returned as dead all-zero columns -- so
`ncol(kernel_res$features)` is usually well below the full combinatorial count of
cell-type pairs. Lower `zero_threshold` (e.g. `0.9`) to also drop features that are
zero in most patients.

#### Raw or normalized features?

With `norm = FALSE` (the default) features are the raw communication strength, which
grows with both the abundance of the two cell types and the expression of their
ligand-receptor pairs. With `norm = TRUE`, RaCInG also builds a baseline in which
every possible ligand-receptor pair is equally strong and reports the ratio of the
two: an enrichment score that does not depend on cell-type abundance and isolates
which pairs communicate more (or less) than the network structure alone predicts.
In the Monte Carlo method the ratio of two simulated estimates is noisier than the
raw value, so budget a larger `Ngraphs` when you use `norm = TRUE` there.

### 3. Run the Monte Carlo method

Use the Monte Carlo workflow when you want simulation-based summaries or uncertainty
estimates from repeated graph realizations. The same `input_data` shortcut is
available here. Simulation cost scales with `Ncells` and `Ngraphs`; the values below
are kept small for a quick illustration.

```{r eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  counts = counts_matrix,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  deconv_method = "Quantiseq",
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  nPatients = 3,
  communication_type = "D",
  Ncells = 100,
  Ngraphs = 10,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm = TRUE
)

# Or from pre-computed inputs:
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data = input,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  communication_type = "D",
  Ncells = 100,
  Ngraphs = 10,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm = TRUE
)

head(mc_res$output$mean[, 1:5])
```

`mc_res$output` holds the per-patient mean (`mean`) and standard deviation (`sd`)
across the simulated graphs. The raw simulations (`<file_name>.out`, and
`<file_name>_norm.out` with `norm = TRUE`) and the processed features
(`<file_name>.csv`, `<file_name>_sd.csv`) are also written to `output_folder`; they
can be re-read later with `Read_Sim_Output()` and `compute_results_processing()`.

`communication_type` can also be `"GSCC"` (the share of cells, per cell type, in the
giant strongly connected component) or both, `c("D", "GSCC")`. Both are then
extracted from the *same* simulated graphs, instead of re-simulating a fresh set of
graphs per type -- graph generation, not feature extraction, is the expensive part of
a Monte Carlo run:

```{r eval = FALSE}
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = c("D", "GSCC"),
  Ncells = 100,
  Ngraphs = 10,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm = TRUE,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan"
)

# output is now a named list, one entry per requested type
names(mc_res$output)
head(mc_res$output$D$mean[, 1:5])
```

Patients are independent of each other, so larger runs can be parallelized across
cores with `ncores` (via `parallel`/`doParallel`/`foreach`, so it works the same way
on Windows, macOS, and Linux):

```{r eval = FALSE}
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = "D",
  Ncells = 500,
  Ngraphs = 100,
  Ndegree = 20,
  ncores = 4,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan"
)
```

### 4. Compare clinical groups

Once features are available in a patient-by-feature matrix, use the built-in Wilcoxon
workflow to compare groups. `wilcox_group_test()` reports, per feature and per pair
of groups, the Wilcoxon statistic, fold change, and (jointly) FDR-adjusted p-value;
`top_features_plot()` shows the top up/down features by `log2(fold change)` as a
ranked bar chart.

```{r eval = FALSE}
# One label per patient (row of the feature matrix); replace this placeholder
# with your own clinical annotation, e.g. response to therapy.
grouping <- rep(c("Responder", "Non-responder"), length.out = nrow(kernel_res$features))
wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
head(wilcox_results)
top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 15)
```

With more than two groups, every pairwise comparison is run automatically; subset
`wilcox_results` by `Comparison` (or pass a two-group subset to `top_features_plot()`) to
inspect one pair at a time.

### 5. Correlate features with a continuous score

If you have a continuous per-patient score (e.g. an immune response or survival
score), `correlate_features_with_score()` reports the Spearman correlation between
every feature and the score, pooled across all patients and, optionally, within
groups. `correlation_plot()` shows the top positive and negative correlations.

```{r eval = FALSE}
response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
head(corr_results)
correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)
```

## Understanding the input files

RaCInG requires four matrices and associated label vectors that describe the
cell-cell communication landscape for a cohort of patients. The table below
summarises each component:

| Component | Dimensions | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lmatrix** | cell types × ligands | Binary compatibility matrix: `1` if that ligand is expressed above `expr_threshold` in that cell type, `0` otherwise. Rows are cell types; columns are ligands. |
| **Rmatrix** | cell types × receptors | Binary compatibility matrix: `1` if that receptor is expressed above `expr_threshold` in that cell type, `0` otherwise. Same row order as `Lmatrix`. |
| **Cmatrix** | patients × cell types | Cell-type fraction for each patient. Each row sums to 1. |
| **LRmatrix** | ligands × receptors × patients | 3-D tensor of ligand–receptor interaction weights. Each patient slice is normalised to sum to 1. |
| **celltypes** | character vector | Alphabetically sorted cell-type names (shared across L, R, and C). |
| **ligands** | character vector | Ligand names matching the columns of `Lmatrix` and the first axis of `LRmatrix`. |
| **receptors** | character vector | Receptor names matching the columns of `Rmatrix` and the second axis of `LRmatrix`. |
| **Sign_matrix** | ligands × receptors | Placeholder for stimulatory (+1) / inhibitory (−1) interaction signs; all zeros (unknown) by default. Not used by the current kernel or Monte Carlo features. |

These inputs are typically generated by `prepare_input_files()` from a raw
counts matrix, or they can be assembled manually from pre-existing deconvolution
and prior-network data. The bundled `skcm_example` dataset provides a ready-made
example of this structure.

### Inspecting the example inputs

```{r}
library(RaCInG)
data(skcm_example)

# Overall structure
str(skcm_example, max.level = 1)
```

```{r}
# Lmatrix: 9 cell types × 276 ligands
dim(skcm_example$Lmatrix)
skcm_example$Lmatrix[1:4, 1:5]
```

```{r}
# Rmatrix: 9 cell types × 298 receptors
dim(skcm_example$Rmatrix)
skcm_example$Rmatrix[1:4, 1:5]
```

```{r}
# Cmatrix: 10 patients × 9 cell types (rows sum to 1)
dim(skcm_example$Cmatrix)
skcm_example$Cmatrix[1:4, ]
```

```{r}
# LRmatrix: 276 ligands × 298 receptors × 10 patients (3-D tensor)
dim(skcm_example$LRmatrix)
# First patient slice, top-left corner:
skcm_example$LRmatrix[1:4, 1:4, 1]
```

```{r}
# Label vectors
skcm_example$celltypes
head(skcm_example$ligands, 10)
head(skcm_example$receptors, 10)
```

## Running with the bundled example data

The `skcm_example` list shown above can be passed directly to the kernel or Monte
Carlo workflows via the `input_data` parameter, and to the statistical analysis
functions once features have been computed.

### Kernel method on the example data

```{r}
kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  input_data   = skcm_example,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  communication_type = "D",
  norm = TRUE
)

head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])
```

### Decomposing a score into ligand-receptor pairs

`compute_kernel()` sums over every ligand-receptor pair to produce one score per
cell-type pair, so that score alone can't tell you which ligand-receptor pairs drove
it. `computeLRContributions()` recovers that breakdown for one sender-receiver pair
(exploiting that the kernel formula is linear in `LRmatrix`, so each pair's
contribution can be computed directly and sums back exactly to the original score),
and `plotLRContributions()` shows the top contributors as a LIANA-style dot plot (dot
size = share of that pair's total score, color = raw contribution).

```{r, fig.alt = "Dot plot of the top ligand-receptor pairs contributing to Tumor and CD8+ T communication, per patient; dot size is the share of the total score and color the raw contribution."}
lr_contrib <- computeLRContributions(
  Lmatrix = skcm_example$Lmatrix, Rmatrix = skcm_example$Rmatrix,
  Cmatrix = skcm_example$Cmatrix, LRmatrix = skcm_example$LRmatrix,
  celltypes = skcm_example$celltypes, sender = "Tumor", receiver = "CD8+ T"
)
head(lr_contrib)
plotLRContributions(lr_contrib, top_n = 10)
```

### Statistical analysis on the example data

The example data has no clinical annotation, so for illustration patients are split
by their CD8+ T-cell infiltration (above vs below the median). In your own data, use
a real clinical variable such as response to therapy. (With only 10 patients many
values are tied, so `wilcox.test()` warns that it cannot compute exact p-values;
those warnings are hidden here.)

```{r, warning = FALSE, fig.alt = "Ranked bar chart of the direct-communication features most up- and down-regulated in CD8-high versus CD8-low patients."}
cd8 <- skcm_example$Cmatrix[, "CD8+ T"]
grouping <- ifelse(cd8 > median(cd8), "CD8_high", "CD8_low")
wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
head(wilcox_results)
top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 10)
```

For a continuous score, a random placeholder is used below; replace it with a
per-patient score of your own (e.g. an immune-response signature).

```{r, fig.alt = "Diverging bar chart of the features with the strongest positive and negative Spearman correlations with the score."}
set.seed(1)
response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
head(corr_results)
correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)
```

### Monte Carlo method on the example data

The settings below are deliberately tiny so the example runs in seconds; real
analyses use thousands of cells (`Ncells`) and around 100 graphs (`Ngraphs`) per
patient.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data   = skcm_example,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name     = "skcm_example",
  nPatients     = 2,
  communication_type = c("D", "GSCC"),
  Ncells  = 100,
  Ngraphs = 5,
  Ndegree = 3
)

# Direct communication: mean and standard deviation across the simulated graphs
head(mc_res$output$D$mean[, 1:5])
head(mc_res$output$D$sd[, 1:5])

# Fraction of all cells that belong to the GSCC, per cell type
mc_res$output$GSCC$mean
```

## Notes

- `compute_racing_kernel()` and `compute_racing_montecarlo()` are the main entry points.
- The kernel method computes direct communication only; GSCC is available with the
  Monte Carlo method. Wedges and triangles are no longer part of RaCInG.
- Both accept an `input_data` argument with pre-computed matrices (as returned by
  `prepare_input_files()`), which skips all preprocessing.

480	#'   Columns keep multideconv's names: subgroups (`"B.cells_Subgroup.1"`)
481	#'   and unclustered features (`"Quantiseq_TIL10_B.cells"`). When you supply
482	#'   `deconv` yourself, its rows must be exactly `colnames(counts)`, in the same
483	#'   order, and its columns should be named with multideconv's standardized
484	#'   cell-type nomenclature (`multideconv::get_cell_type_nomenclature()`); a
485	#'   warning lists any that aren't.
486	#' @param cc_network Optional ligand-receptor prior network. If omitted, it is
487	#'   retrieved via `liana::get_curated_omni()` (a curated, OmniPath-backed
488	#'   consensus of CellPhoneDB/CellChatDB/ICELLNET/connectomeDB2020/CellTalkDB)
489	#'   the first time this is called, then cached indefinitely as an RDS file
490	#'   under `tools::R_user_dir("RaCInG", "cache")` and loaded from there on every
491	#'   subsequent call -- avoiding a live network round-trip (and its associated
492	#'   transient-failure risk) on every invocation. Delete that cache file to
493	#'   force a refresh from OmniPath.
494	#' @param fun_LR Function combining a ligand's and receptor's expression
495	#'   values (as a length-2 vector) into one interaction strength. Default
496	#'   `min`: the weaker-expressed partner limits the interaction. Any function
497	#'   collapsing 2 values to 1 works, e.g. `prod` for the product of the two
498	#'   instead.
499	#' @param cell_expr_profile Optional gene-by-cell-type expression profile
500	#'   matrix. If omitted, it is estimated via per-gene non-negative least
501	#'   squares -- per method-signature block, then merged according to the
502	#'   multideconv subgroup analysis, when `deconv` is auto-computed (see
503	#'   `.estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups()`), or directly from the
504	#'   supplied `deconv` otherwise (see `.estimate_expression_profiles_samples()`).
505	#' @param source,target Column names to use as ligand and receptor identifiers when `cc_network` is supplied.
506	#' @param deconv_method Deconvolution method(s) passed to `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()`.
507	#'   Default: the default set of `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` -- Quantiseq,
508	#'   CIBERSORTx (CBSX), EpiDISH, DeconRNASeq and DWLS, each with all its signatures --
509	#'   whose estimates are combined into cell subgroups by
510	#'   `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()`. CBSX needs `cbsx.name` and
511	#'   `cbsx.token`; without them multideconv skips it with a warning. With several
512	#'   methods each harmonized feature is one cell type of the networks (often more than
513	#'   a hundred), so wedges, triangles and the Monte Carlo method need much more memory
514	#'   and time than with a single method (e.g. `deconv_method = "Quantiseq"`).
515	#' @param cbsx.name,cbsx.token Optional credentials forwarded to the deconvolution workflow.
516	#' @param file_name File stem used when exporting the generated CSV files.
517	#' @param signed Logical; if `TRUE`, also try to load a sign matrix from `output_folder`.
518	#'
519	#' @param already_normalized Logical; if `TRUE`, `counts` is treated as
520	#'   already TPM-normalized, **linear scale, not logged**, and the internal
521	#'   `ADImpute::NormalizeTPM()` gene-length/library-size normalization is
522	#'   skipped. Use this for datasets where only pre-normalized expression is
523	#'   available (e.g. public cohorts distributed as log2(TPM+1) matrices with
524	#'   no raw counts -- convert those back to linear scale, e.g. `2^x - 1`,
525	#'   before passing them here) -- applying `NormalizeTPM()` to already-
526	#'   normalized data would re-apply its gene-length correction on top of the
527	#'   original normalization, distorting relative gene expression levels.
528	#'   Emits a warning, since `expr_threshold` below is only meaningful if this
529	#'   linear-scale assumption holds -- comparing a log-scale value against it
530	#'   would silently apply the wrong cutoff.
531	#'
532	#' @param expr_threshold Minimum expression value, in linear-scale TPM (in
533	#'   `cell_expr_profile` units), a ligand or receptor must reach in its
534	#'   sending/receiving cell type for that ligand-receptor-celltype triple to
535	#'   be kept in `CC_table`.
536	#'
537	#' @param LR_activity Optional. By default (`NULL`) the per-patient strength of a
538	#'   ligand-receptor pair is `fun_LR` of the ligand's and receptor's bulk
539	#'   expression. Set it to use their signalling *activity* instead: either
540	#'   `"activity"` (computes it with [compute_LR_activity()], MOON-based; slow,
541	#'   roughly 10 seconds per patient), or a precomputed gene-by-sample matrix of
542	#'   activities such as the one [compute_LR_activity()] returns (columns must be the
543	#'   samples of `counts`). Negative activities are set to 0. Only the per-patient
544	#'   strength changes; which cell types can send/receive each ligand/receptor
545	#'   (`expr_threshold`) is still decided by expression.
546	#'
547	#' @return A named list with the processed input matrices and their labels:
548	#'   `Lmatrix`, `Rmatrix`, `Cmatrix` (normalised), `LRmatrix` (3-D tensor),
549	#'   `celltypes`, `ligands`, `receptors`, `Sign_matrix`, and `CC_table`.
550	#' @export
551	prepare_input_files <- function(counts, output_folder = "Results/", deconv = NULL, cc_network = NULL, fun_LR = min,
552	                                cell_expr_profile = NULL, source = "source_genesymbol", target = "target_genesymbol",
553	                                deconv_method = c("Quantiseq", "CBSX", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS"), cbsx.name = NULL, cbsx.token = NULL, file_name = NULL,
554	                                signed = FALSE, already_normalized = FALSE, expr_threshold = 10, LR_activity = NULL){
555	
556	  if (is.null(file_name)) {
557	    file_name <- "RaCInG_input"
558	  }
559	
560	  .check_installed_packages(if (already_normalized) "multideconv" else c("ADImpute", "multideconv"))
561	  if (already_normalized) {
562	    warning(
563	      "already_normalized = TRUE: 'counts' is assumed to already be linear-scale TPM. ",
564	      "expr_threshold (default ", expr_threshold, ") is compared against this scale -- ",
565	      "if 'counts' is actually log-transformed (e.g. log2(TPM+1)), that comparison is ",
566	      "wrong; convert back to linear TPM first or set expr_threshold accordingly.",
567	      call. = FALSE
568	    )
569	    counts.tpm <- as.matrix(counts)
570	  } else {
571	    counts.tpm <- ADImpute::NormalizeTPM(counts)
572	  }
573	  counts.log.tpm <- log2(counts.tpm + 1)
574	
575	  cat("Calculating deconvolution estimates...\n")
576	
577	  ## C-matrix
578	  # deconv_wide/subgroups stay NULL on the user-supplied-deconv path below --
579	  # there's no known method/signature block structure to fit expression
580	  # profiles per block, so that path falls back to treating the whole matrix
581	  # as one composition (see the expression-profile step further down).
582	  deconv_wide <- NULL
583	  subgroups <- NULL
584	  if (is.null(deconv)) {
585	    deconv_wide <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution(
586	      counts.tpm,
587	      normalized = FALSE,
588	      methods = deconv_method,
589	      credentials.mail = cbsx.name,
590	      credentials.token = cbsx.token,
591	      file_name = file_name
592	    )
593	
594	    ## Same samples as counts, in counts' column order (the LR matrix follows that order)
595	    if (!setequal(rownames(deconv_wide), colnames(counts))) {
596	      stop("Patient names in deconvolution estimates do not match those in the counts matrix.")
597	    }
598	    deconv_wide <- deconv_wide[colnames(counts), , drop = FALSE]
599	
600	    cat("Identifying cell type subgroups...\n")
601	    subgroups <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis(deconv_wide)
602	    deconv <- subgroups[["Deconvolution matrix"]]
603	  } else {
604	    cat("Using provided deconvolution estimates...\n")
605	    # Cmatrix rows follow rownames(deconv) and the LR matrix follows colnames(counts),
606	    # and they are later paired by position -- so they must be identical, in order.
607	    if (!identical(rownames(deconv), colnames(counts))) {
608	      if (!is.null(rownames(deconv)) && setequal(rownames(deconv), colnames(counts))) {
609	        stop("rownames(deconv) contain the same samples as colnames(counts) but in a different order; ",
610	             "reorder it first, e.g. deconv[colnames(counts), , drop = FALSE].", call. = FALSE)
611	      }
612	      stop("rownames(deconv) must be exactly the samples in colnames(counts), in the same order ",
613	           "(missing from deconv: ", length(setdiff(colnames(counts), rownames(deconv))),
614	           ", not in counts: ", length(setdiff(rownames(deconv), colnames(counts))), ").", call. = FALSE)
615	    }
616	    .warn_nonstandard_celltypes(colnames(deconv))
617	  }
618	
619	  ## Cell type expression profiles
620	  cat("\nEstimating cell type expression profiles...\n")
621	  if (is.null(cell_expr_profile)) {
622	    .check_installed_packages("nnls")
623	    if (!is.null(deconv_wide)) {
624	      # Fit one profile per method-signature block (each a valid composition),
625	      # then merge according to whichever subgroups multideconv formed --
626	      # never fit NNLS directly on the merged Deconvolution matrix (`deconv`),
627	      # which stitches together representatives from different blocks and is
628	      # not itself a valid composition. See .estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups().
629	      cell_expr_profile <- .estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups(counts.tpm, deconv_wide, subgroups)
630	    } else {
631	      # A user-supplied deconv has no known block structure -- treat it as one
632	      # composition, as before.
633	      cell_expr_profile <- .estimate_expression_profiles_samples(counts.tpm, deconv)
634	    }
635	  }
636	
637	  ## Prior knowledge network CC
638	  cat("Processing cell-cell interaction network...\n")
639	  if (is.null(cc_network)) {
640	    .check_installed_packages(c("OmnipathR", "liana"))
641	    cache_dir <- tools::R_user_dir("RaCInG", "cache")
642	    cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, "curated_omni_network.rds")
643	    if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
644	      cc_network <- readRDS(cache_file)
645	    } else {
646	      # get_curated_omni()'s underlying calls hit OmnipathR's own on-disk cache for
647	      # most of the network data, but at least one internal step (parameter
648	      # validation against OmnipathR::resources()) always makes a live request
649	      # regardless -- so this whole result is still subject to transient network
650	      # failures on every fresh R session unless cached at this level too.
651	      cc_network <- liana::get_curated_omni() %>%
652	        dplyr::filter(category_intercell_source %in% c("cell_surface_ligand", "ligand") &
653	                      category_intercell_target %in% c("receptor", "adhesion")) %>%
654	        liana::decomplexify(columns = c("source_genesymbol", "target_genesymbol"))
655	      dir.create(cache_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
656	      saveRDS(cc_network, cache_file)
657	    }
658	  } else {
659	    cc_network <- cc_network %>%
660	      dplyr::mutate(source_genesymbol = .data[[source]], target_genesymbol = .data[[target]])
661	  }
662	  
663	  ## Subset expression for LR pairs (keep only interactions present in cell_expr_profile)
664	  keep <- integer()
665	  for (i in seq_len(nrow(cc_network))) {
666	    ligand  <- cc_network$source_genesymbol[i]
667	    receptor <- cc_network$target_genesymbol[i]
668	    if (ligand %in% rownames(cell_expr_profile) & receptor %in% rownames(cell_expr_profile)) {
669	      keep <- c(keep, i)
670	    }
671	  }
672	  cc_interations_sub <- cc_network[keep, , drop = FALSE]
673	  
674	  ## Build CC table (Sender x each LR pair x Receiver)
675	  ## Vectorized and processed one sender at a time: the previous implementation
676	  ## built one data.frame per (cell_type, LR pair) via nested
677	  ## do.call(rbind, lapply(...)) calls, i.e. O(n_celltypes * n_LR_pairs) tiny
678	  ## data.frames rbound together. With many deconvolution features (e.g.
679	  ## combining several deconvolution methods) n_celltypes can reach 100+, and
680	  ## with a curated LR network of several thousand pairs this produced
681	  ## hundreds of thousands of rbind pieces and tens of millions of rows, slow
682	  ## enough (tens of minutes) and memory-heavy enough to crash on typical
683	  ## machines. A single vectorized pass across the full sender x LR x receiver
684	  ## grid fixed the speed but still peaks at O(n_celltypes^2 * n_LR_pairs)
685	  ## elements transiently (~15GB observed with 122 cell types, i.e. the
686	  ## machine's entire RAM) before the expression-threshold filter shrinks it
687	  ## back down. Building one sender's full receiver grid at a time and
688	  ## filtering immediately keeps peak memory at O(n_celltypes * n_LR_pairs)
689	  ## instead, independent of how many senders there are.
690	  celltypes_all <- colnames(cell_expr_profile)
691	  n_ct <- length(celltypes_all)
692	  n_lr <- nrow(cc_interations_sub)
693	  cell_expr_mat <- as.matrix(cell_expr_profile)
694	  L_all <- cc_interations_sub$source_genesymbol
695	  R_all <- cc_interations_sub$target_genesymbol
696	  L_row <- match(L_all, rownames(cell_expr_mat))
697	  R_row <- match(R_all, rownames(cell_expr_mat))
698	
699	  lr_idx_rep       <- rep(seq_len(n_lr), each = n_ct)
700	  receiver_idx_rep <- rep(seq_len(n_ct), times = n_lr)
701	  R_row_rep        <- R_row[lr_idx_rep]
702	
703	  ccc_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_ct), function(s) {
704	    Expr_Ligand   <- cell_expr_mat[L_row[lr_idx_rep], s]
705	    Expr_Receptor <- cell_expr_mat[cbind(R_row_rep, receiver_idx_rep)]
706	    keep <- Expr_Ligand >= expr_threshold & Expr_Receptor >= expr_threshold ## Keep only pairs expressed above threshold
707	    data.frame(
708	      Sender = rep(celltypes_all[s], sum(keep)),
709	      Ligand = L_all[lr_idx_rep[keep]],
710	      Expr_Ligand = Expr_Ligand[keep],
711	      Receiver = celltypes_all[receiver_idx_rep[keep]],
712	      Receptor = R_all[lr_idx_rep[keep]],
713	      Expr_Receptor = Expr_Receptor[keep]
714	    )
715	  }))
716	
717	  ## Use the actual matched (Ligand, Receptor) pairs present in ccc_table --
718	  ## previously this zipped unique(Ligand) with unique(Receptor) positionally,
719	  ## silently mismatching real pairs whenever the two vectors had different
720	  ## lengths (recycling warning: "number of columns of result is not a

#'   Columns keep multideconv's names: subgroups (`"B.cells_Subgroup.1"`)
#'   and unclustered features (`"Quantiseq_TIL10_B.cells"`). When you supply
#'   `deconv` yourself, its rows must be exactly `colnames(counts)`, in the same
#'   order, and its columns should be named with multideconv's standardized
#'   cell-type nomenclature (`multideconv::get_cell_type_nomenclature()`); a
#'   warning lists any that aren't.
#' @param cc_network Optional ligand-receptor prior network. If omitted, it is
#'   retrieved via `liana::get_curated_omni()` (a curated, OmniPath-backed
#'   consensus of CellPhoneDB/CellChatDB/ICELLNET/connectomeDB2020/CellTalkDB)
#'   the first time this is called, then cached indefinitely as an RDS file
#'   under `tools::R_user_dir("RaCInG", "cache")` and loaded from there on every
#'   subsequent call -- avoiding a live network round-trip (and its associated
#'   transient-failure risk) on every invocation. Delete that cache file to
#'   force a refresh from OmniPath.
#' @param fun_LR Function combining a ligand's and receptor's expression
#'   values (as a length-2 vector) into one interaction strength. Default
#'   `min`: the weaker-expressed partner limits the interaction. Any function
#'   collapsing 2 values to 1 works, e.g. `prod` for the product of the two
#'   instead.
#' @param cell_expr_profile Optional gene-by-cell-type expression profile
#'   matrix. If omitted, it is estimated via per-gene non-negative least
#'   squares -- per method-signature block, then merged according to the
#'   multideconv subgroup analysis, when `deconv` is auto-computed (see
#'   `.estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups()`), or directly from the
#'   supplied `deconv` otherwise (see `.estimate_expression_profiles_samples()`).
#' @param source,target Column names to use as ligand and receptor identifiers when `cc_network` is supplied.
#' @param deconv_method Deconvolution method(s) passed to `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()`.
#'   Default: the default set of `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` -- Quantiseq,
#'   CIBERSORTx (CBSX), EpiDISH, DeconRNASeq and DWLS, each with all its signatures --
#'   whose estimates are combined into cell subgroups by
#'   `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()`. CBSX needs `cbsx.name` and
#'   `cbsx.token`; without them multideconv skips it with a warning. With several
#'   methods each harmonized feature is one cell type of the networks (often more than
#'   a hundred), so wedges, triangles and the Monte Carlo method need much more memory
#'   and time than with a single method (e.g. `deconv_method = "Quantiseq"`).
#' @param cbsx.name,cbsx.token Optional credentials forwarded to the deconvolution workflow.
#' @param file_name File stem used when exporting the generated CSV files.
#' @param signed Logical; if `TRUE`, also try to load a sign matrix from `output_folder`.
#'
#' @param already_normalized Logical; if `TRUE`, `counts` is treated as
#'   already TPM-normalized, **linear scale, not logged**, and the internal
#'   `ADImpute::NormalizeTPM()` gene-length/library-size normalization is
#'   skipped. Use this for datasets where only pre-normalized expression is
#'   available (e.g. public cohorts distributed as log2(TPM+1) matrices with
#'   no raw counts -- convert those back to linear scale, e.g. `2^x - 1`,
#'   before passing them here) -- applying `NormalizeTPM()` to already-
#'   normalized data would re-apply its gene-length correction on top of the
#'   original normalization, distorting relative gene expression levels.
#'   Emits a warning, since `expr_threshold` below is only meaningful if this
#'   linear-scale assumption holds -- comparing a log-scale value against it
#'   would silently apply the wrong cutoff.
#'
#' @param expr_threshold Minimum expression value, in linear-scale TPM (in
#'   `cell_expr_profile` units), a ligand or receptor must reach in its
#'   sending/receiving cell type for that ligand-receptor-celltype triple to
#'   be kept in `CC_table`.
#'
#' @param LR_activity Optional. By default (`NULL`) the per-patient strength of a
#'   ligand-receptor pair is `fun_LR` of the ligand's and receptor's bulk
#'   expression. Set it to use their signalling *activity* instead: either
#'   `"activity"` (computes it with [compute_LR_activity()], MOON-based; slow,
#'   roughly 10 seconds per patient), or a precomputed gene-by-sample matrix of
#'   activities such as the one [compute_LR_activity()] returns (columns must be the
#'   samples of `counts`). Negative activities are set to 0. Only the per-patient
#'   strength changes; which cell types can send/receive each ligand/receptor
#'   (`expr_threshold`) is still decided by expression.
#'
#' @return A named list with the processed input matrices and their labels:
#'   `Lmatrix`, `Rmatrix`, `Cmatrix` (normalised), `LRmatrix` (3-D tensor),
#'   `celltypes`, `ligands`, `receptors`, `Sign_matrix`, and `CC_table`.
#' @export
prepare_input_files <- function(counts, output_folder = "Results/", deconv = NULL, cc_network = NULL, fun_LR = min,
                                cell_expr_profile = NULL, source = "source_genesymbol", target = "target_genesymbol",
                                deconv_method = c("Quantiseq", "CBSX", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS"), cbsx.name = NULL, cbsx.token = NULL, file_name = NULL,
                                signed = FALSE, already_normalized = FALSE, expr_threshold = 10, LR_activity = NULL){

  if (is.null(file_name)) {
    file_name <- "RaCInG_input"
  }

  .check_installed_packages(if (already_normalized) "multideconv" else c("ADImpute", "multideconv"))
  if (already_normalized) {
    warning(
      "already_normalized = TRUE: 'counts' is assumed to already be linear-scale TPM. ",
      "expr_threshold (default ", expr_threshold, ") is compared against this scale -- ",
      "if 'counts' is actually log-transformed (e.g. log2(TPM+1)), that comparison is ",
      "wrong; convert back to linear TPM first or set expr_threshold accordingly.",
      call. = FALSE
    )
    counts.tpm <- as.matrix(counts)
  } else {
    counts.tpm <- ADImpute::NormalizeTPM(counts)
  }
  counts.log.tpm <- log2(counts.tpm + 1)

  cat("Calculating deconvolution estimates...\n")

  ## C-matrix
  # deconv_wide/subgroups stay NULL on the user-supplied-deconv path below --
  # there's no known method/signature block structure to fit expression
  # profiles per block, so that path falls back to treating the whole matrix
  # as one composition (see the expression-profile step further down).
  deconv_wide <- NULL
  subgroups <- NULL
  if (is.null(deconv)) {
    deconv_wide <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution(
      counts.tpm,
      normalized = FALSE,
      methods = deconv_method,
      credentials.mail = cbsx.name,
      credentials.token = cbsx.token,
      file_name = file_name
    )

    ## Same samples as counts, in counts' column order (the LR matrix follows that order)
    if (!setequal(rownames(deconv_wide), colnames(counts))) {
      stop("Patient names in deconvolution estimates do not match those in the counts matrix.")
    }
    deconv_wide <- deconv_wide[colnames(counts), , drop = FALSE]

    cat("Identifying cell type subgroups...\n")
    subgroups <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis(deconv_wide)
    deconv <- subgroups[["Deconvolution matrix"]]
  } else {
    cat("Using provided deconvolution estimates...\n")
    # Cmatrix rows follow rownames(deconv) and the LR matrix follows colnames(counts),
    # and they are later paired by position -- so they must be identical, in order.
    if (!identical(rownames(deconv), colnames(counts))) {
      if (!is.null(rownames(deconv)) && setequal(rownames(deconv), colnames(counts))) {
        stop("rownames(deconv) contain the same samples as colnames(counts) but in a different order; ",
             "reorder it first, e.g. deconv[colnames(counts), , drop = FALSE].", call. = FALSE)
      }
      stop("rownames(deconv) must be exactly the samples in colnames(counts), in the same order ",
           "(missing from deconv: ", length(setdiff(colnames(counts), rownames(deconv))),
           ", not in counts: ", length(setdiff(rownames(deconv), colnames(counts))), ").", call. = FALSE)
    }
    .warn_nonstandard_celltypes(colnames(deconv))
  }

  ## Cell type expression profiles
  cat("\nEstimating cell type expression profiles...\n")
  if (is.null(cell_expr_profile)) {
    .check_installed_packages("nnls")
    if (!is.null(deconv_wide)) {
      # Fit one profile per method-signature block (each a valid composition),
      # then merge according to whichever subgroups multideconv formed --
      # never fit NNLS directly on the merged Deconvolution matrix (`deconv`),
      # which stitches together representatives from different blocks and is
      # not itself a valid composition. See .estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups().
      cell_expr_profile <- .estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups(counts.tpm, deconv_wide, subgroups)
    } else {
      # A user-supplied deconv has no known block structure -- treat it as one
      # composition, as before.
      cell_expr_profile <- .estimate_expression_profiles_samples(counts.tpm, deconv)
    }
  }

  ## Prior knowledge network CC
  cat("Processing cell-cell interaction network...\n")
  if (is.null(cc_network)) {
    .check_installed_packages(c("OmnipathR", "liana"))
    cache_dir <- tools::R_user_dir("RaCInG", "cache")
    cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, "curated_omni_network.rds")
    if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
      cc_network <- readRDS(cache_file)
    } else {
      # get_curated_omni()'s underlying calls hit OmnipathR's own on-disk cache for
      # most of the network data, but at least one internal step (parameter
      # validation against OmnipathR::resources()) always makes a live request
      # regardless -- so this whole result is still subject to transient network
      # failures on every fresh R session unless cached at this level too.
      cc_network <- liana::get_curated_omni() %>%
        dplyr::filter(category_intercell_source %in% c("cell_surface_ligand", "ligand") &
                      category_intercell_target %in% c("receptor", "adhesion")) %>%
        liana::decomplexify(columns = c("source_genesymbol", "target_genesymbol"))
      dir.create(cache_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
      saveRDS(cc_network, cache_file)
    }
  } else {
    cc_network <- cc_network %>%
      dplyr::mutate(source_genesymbol = .data[[source]], target_genesymbol = .data[[target]])
  }
  
  ## Subset expression for LR pairs (keep only interactions present in cell_expr_profile)
  keep <- integer()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(cc_network))) {
    ligand  <- cc_network$source_genesymbol[i]
    receptor <- cc_network$target_genesymbol[i]
    if (ligand %in% rownames(cell_expr_profile) & receptor %in% rownames(cell_expr_profile)) {
      keep <- c(keep, i)
    }
  }
  cc_interations_sub <- cc_network[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  
  ## Build CC table (Sender x each LR pair x Receiver)
  ## Vectorized and processed one sender at a time: the previous implementation
  ## built one data.frame per (cell_type, LR pair) via nested
  ## do.call(rbind, lapply(...)) calls, i.e. O(n_celltypes * n_LR_pairs) tiny
  ## data.frames rbound together. With many deconvolution features (e.g.
  ## combining several deconvolution methods) n_celltypes can reach 100+, and
  ## with a curated LR network of several thousand pairs this produced
  ## hundreds of thousands of rbind pieces and tens of millions of rows, slow
  ## enough (tens of minutes) and memory-heavy enough to crash on typical
  ## machines. A single vectorized pass across the full sender x LR x receiver
  ## grid fixed the speed but still peaks at O(n_celltypes^2 * n_LR_pairs)
  ## elements transiently (~15GB observed with 122 cell types, i.e. the
  ## machine's entire RAM) before the expression-threshold filter shrinks it
  ## back down. Building one sender's full receiver grid at a time and
  ## filtering immediately keeps peak memory at O(n_celltypes * n_LR_pairs)
  ## instead, independent of how many senders there are.
  celltypes_all <- colnames(cell_expr_profile)
  n_ct <- length(celltypes_all)
  n_lr <- nrow(cc_interations_sub)
  cell_expr_mat <- as.matrix(cell_expr_profile)
  L_all <- cc_interations_sub$source_genesymbol
  R_all <- cc_interations_sub$target_genesymbol
  L_row <- match(L_all, rownames(cell_expr_mat))
  R_row <- match(R_all, rownames(cell_expr_mat))

  lr_idx_rep       <- rep(seq_len(n_lr), each = n_ct)
  receiver_idx_rep <- rep(seq_len(n_ct), times = n_lr)
  R_row_rep        <- R_row[lr_idx_rep]

  ccc_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_ct), function(s) {
    Expr_Ligand   <- cell_expr_mat[L_row[lr_idx_rep], s]
    Expr_Receptor <- cell_expr_mat[cbind(R_row_rep, receiver_idx_rep)]
    keep <- Expr_Ligand >= expr_threshold & Expr_Receptor >= expr_threshold ## Keep only pairs expressed above threshold
    data.frame(
      Sender = rep(celltypes_all[s], sum(keep)),
      Ligand = L_all[lr_idx_rep[keep]],
      Expr_Ligand = Expr_Ligand[keep],
      Receiver = celltypes_all[receiver_idx_rep[keep]],
      Receptor = R_all[lr_idx_rep[keep]],
      Expr_Receptor = Expr_Receptor[keep]
    )
  }))

  ## Use the actual matched (Ligand, Receptor) pairs present in ccc_table --
  ## previously this zipped unique(Ligand) with unique(Receptor) positionally,
  ## silently mismatching real pairs whenever the two vectors had different
  ## lengths (recycling warning: "number of columns of result is not a
  ## multiple of vector length").
  lr_pairs_df <- unique(ccc_table[, c("Ligand", "Receptor")])
  ligands <- lr_pairs_df$Ligand
  receptors <- lr_pairs_df$Receptor
  LR_pairs <- paste0(ligands, "_", receptors)

  ## LR-matrix: compute fun(L, R) per sample using counts (rows=genes, cols=samples): Default min(L,R)
  ## With LR_activity, the ligand/receptor activity replaces their expression
  cat("Computing LR matrix...\n")
  LR_values <- counts.log.tpm
  if (!is.null(LR_activity)) {
    LR_values <- .resolve_LR_activity(LR_activity, counts.log.tpm, cc_interations_sub)
  }
  pos_lr <- match(c(rbind(ligands, receptors)), rownames(LR_values))
  pos_lr <- matrix(pos_lr, nrow = 2)
  
  LR_matrix <- apply(pos_lr, 2, function(idx) {
    if (any(is.na(idx))) {
      return(rep(NA, ncol(LR_values)))

#'
#' # Enrichment ratio over a uniform ligand-receptor baseline
#' res_norm <- compute_racing_kernel(input_data = skcm_example, norm = TRUE)
#' head(res_norm$features[, 1:4])
compute_racing_kernel = function(counts = NULL, output_folder = "Results/", deconv = NULL, cc_network = NULL, fun_LR = min,
                                 cell_expr_profile = NULL, source = "source_genesymbol", target = "target_genesymbol", signed = FALSE,
                                 deconv_method = c("Quantiseq", "CBSX", "Epidish", "DeconRNASeq", "DWLS"), cbsx.name = NULL, cbsx.token = NULL, file_name = NULL, nPatients = "all",
                                 communication_type = "D", norm = FALSE, pt_idx = NULL, remove_direction = TRUE,
                                 input_data = NULL, zero_threshold = 1, expr_threshold = 10, already_normalized = FALSE, LR_activity = NULL) {

  .check_kernel_communication_type(communication_type)

  if (is.null(file_name)) {
    file_name <- "RaCInG_input"
  }

  if (!is.null(input_data)) {
    cat("Using pre-computed input matrices; skipping input generation.\n")
    res <- input_data
  } else {
    if (is.null(counts)) {
      stop("Either 'counts' or 'input_data' must be provided.", call. = FALSE)
    }
    res <- prepare_input_files(counts, output_folder = output_folder, deconv = deconv, cc_network = cc_network, fun_LR = fun_LR,
                               cell_expr_profile = cell_expr_profile, source = source, target = target,
                               deconv_method = deconv_method, cbsx.name = cbsx.name, cbsx.token = cbsx.token, file_name = file_name,
                               signed = signed, already_normalized = already_normalized, expr_threshold = expr_threshold,
                               LR_activity = LR_activity)
  }

  Lmatrix   <- res$Lmatrix
  Rmatrix   <- res$Rmatrix
  Cmatrix    <- res$Cmatrix
  LRmatrix   <- res$LRmatrix
  cellTypes <- res$celltypes
  # Name unnamed patients by their Cmatrix row, so subset runs keep the right labels
  if (is.null(rownames(Cmatrix))) rownames(Cmatrix) <- paste0("Patient_", seq_len(nrow(Cmatrix)))

  if (nPatients == "all") {
    nPatients <- nrow(Cmatrix)
  }

  if(!is.null(pt_idx)){
    cat("Because patient index is provided, nPatients argument will be ignored.\n")
  }else{
    cat("Computing kernel for", nPatients, "patients\n")
    Cmatrix  <- Cmatrix[1:nPatients, , drop = FALSE]
    LRmatrix <- LRmatrix[,,1:nPatients, drop = FALSE]
  }

  # -----------------------------
  # Calculate kernel
  # -----------------------------
  cat("Calculating kernel...\n")
  
  res <- compute_kernel(Lmatrix, Rmatrix, Cmatrix, LRmatrix, normalize = norm)
  kernel_raw <- if (isTRUE(norm)) res$kernel else res
  kernel_norm <- if (isTRUE(norm)) res$kernel_norm else NULL

  # -----------------------------
  # Calculate features
  # -----------------------------
  cat("Calculating features...\n")
  patient_names <- rownames(Cmatrix) # the rows actually used (subset by nPatients above)
  features <- compute_kernel_features(
    kernel = kernel_raw,
    unifKernel = kernel_norm,
    celltypes = cellTypes,
    communication_type = communication_type,
    bundle = remove_direction,
    patient_names = patient_names,
    Dcell = Cmatrix,
    patient_idx = pt_idx,
    zero_threshold = zero_threshold
  )

  return(list(kernel = kernel_raw, kernel_norm = kernel_norm, features = features))

}
